passage:
Dear Diary,
Two new boys came to our class today. Pranjal has round glasses and hardly speaks. He is definitely going to be the topper. You can just tell. Zubin is loud and made the whole back row laugh when Miss was writing on the board, so he must be weak in studies. I chose Pranjal as my partner for the maths quiz. Then Pranjal got three sums wrong, and Zubin got all of them right and even helped me with the last one. I think Zubin was lucky. Tomorrow I will see.
Afreen

qa.q: Who got all the quiz sums right?
qa.a: Zubin got all of them right and even helped with the last one.

qa.q: Why was Afreen so sure Pranjal would be the topper?
qa.a: Afreen felt confident because Pranjal's round glasses and quietness matched Afreen's picture of a topper, so the look felt like proof even before any test.

qa.q: What could Afreen try tomorrow?
qa.a: Afreen could wait to judge until seeing how each boy actually works over a few days, and notice that the quiz already gave real evidence about Zubin.

qa.q: How might Zubin feel if he knew Afreen called him lucky?
qa.a: Zubin might feel unfairly judged, since he got every sum right and even helped, yet was still seen as weak because he is loud.

grounding: Shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses is the topper and the loud boy is weak, then explaining away the quiz result.

passage: At the village school near Sikar, Masterji asked the class to choose two children for the district quiz. Preeti didn't even think. "Mukesh," she said, pointing to the thin boy with thick glasses who sat quietly by the window. Everyone knew clever people looked like that. When someone suggested Vijay, she wrinkled her nose. Vijay was the one who shouted answers without raising his hand and played kabaddi every break. "He only makes noise," she whispered. Masterji held a practice round under the neem tree. Vijay answered eight questions; Mukesh answered two and blushed. Preeti frowned at the chalk tally, as if it had made a mistake.

qa.q: How many questions did Vijay answer in the practice round?
qa.a: Vijay answered eight questions.

qa.q: Why did Preeti frown at the chalk tally?
qa.a: Preeti feels puzzled and a little annoyed, because she had been sure Mukesh's glasses and quietness meant he was clever and Vijay's noise meant he was weak. The tally feels wrong to her rather than informative.

qa.q: How could Masterji help the class choose fairly?
qa.a: Masterji could pick the team from practice rounds like this one and point out that answers, not looks or loudness, show who knows the material.

qa.q: How might Mukesh feel being picked first and then answering only two?
qa.a: Mukesh may feel embarrassed and under pressure, since he was chosen for how he looks rather than for what he knows.

grounding: Shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses must be clever and the loud boy weak, until a practice round disagrees.

passage: On the first day of fourth grade in Kraków, Olga whispered to her friend Ines, "The boy with the glasses, Tomek, he must be a genius. Look how quietly he sits." Ines shrugged. "And that one?" She pointed at Filip, who was drumming on the desk and telling a joke about the teacher's cat. "Definitely bad at maths," Olga said. By Friday the class had done its first test. Filip had the top mark and got a sticker. Tomek had struggled, and at break he told Olga he hated numbers and loved drawing birds. Olga stared at the sticker on Filip's hand for a long time.

qa.q: Who got the top mark in the first test?
qa.a: Filip had the top mark and got a sticker.

qa.q: Why did Olga decide Tomek must be a genius?
qa.a: Olga felt confident because Tomek wore glasses and sat quietly, which matched her picture of a clever child, so his look felt like enough evidence.

qa.q: What could Olga do the next time she meets new classmates?
qa.a: Olga could notice the guess, then wait for real signs, like tests, what people say they love, or how they solve problems, before deciding who is clever.

qa.q: What might Tomek feel if he knew what Olga had first assumed?
qa.a: Tomek might feel pressure or awkwardness at being expected to be a genius at something he dislikes, when what he loves is drawing birds.

grounding: Shows a child judging a quiet boy with glasses as a genius and a loud boy as weak at maths, until the first test shows otherwise.

passage: On day one of the summer chess camp at the community centre, the coach said, "Pick a partner for the puzzle relay." Nilesh, eight, didn't hesitate. He walked straight to Tarun, a thin, quiet boy with big round glasses who was reading the rules sheet. "He looks like a topper," Nilesh whispered to himself. Sonu, a loud boy who had been bouncing a ball, came up hopefully. Nilesh shook his head. "You're too noisy for chess." The relay began. Tarun stared at the first puzzle for ages and got it wrong. At the next table, Sonu shouted "Checkmate!" and slammed down the knight, the fastest in the room. Nilesh's mouth dropped open. At lunch, he went and sat next to Sonu. "How did you see that knight move?"

qa.q: How did Sonu's pair do in the relay?
qa.a: Sonu shouted "Checkmate!" and was the fastest in the room.

qa.q: Why was Nilesh so sure Tarun would be good at chess?
qa.a: Nilesh felt confident because Tarun was quiet, read the rules and wore big round glasses, matching his picture of a topper. The look felt like enough proof.

qa.q: What choice did Nilesh make at lunch, and why was it a good one?
qa.a: He sat next to Sonu and asked how he saw the knight move. That let him learn about Sonu from what Sonu actually did, not from how loud he was.

qa.q: How might Sonu have felt when Nilesh said he was too noisy for chess?
qa.a: Sonu probably felt hurt and left out, being judged before playing a single move.

grounding: A boy at chess camp picks a quiet boy with glasses as his partner because he looks clever, and refuses a loud boy who turns out to be the best.

passage: I'm Nandini, and I help run the Sunday maths club in our building's hall. Here's what I saw with Farida, who's ten. We were forming teams for the number puzzles. Farida marched up to Pranit, who wears thick glasses and barely speaks, and said, "You're with me." Then Gogi, who is loud and was doing cartwheels near the door, asked to join. Farida said, "No thanks, you'll just mess around." I don't know exactly what was in her head. But she kept glancing at Pranit's glasses like they were a guarantee. In the round, Pranit froze; he'd never done this kind of puzzle. Gogi, on another team, finished first and whooped. Farida went red. Later I saw her ask Gogi to show her his trick. Maybe she learned something.

qa.q: What was Gogi doing near the door when he asked to join?
qa.a: He was doing cartwheels near the door.

qa.q: Why might Farida have thought Pranit was a guarantee?
qa.a: He looked like her idea of a clever child, with thick glasses and a quiet manner, so choosing him felt safe. Gogi's loudness seemed to mean he would not be serious.

qa.q: After the round, what did Farida choose to do, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She asked Gogi to show her his trick. That shows she was willing to learn from what she saw rather than stick to her first guess.

qa.q: How might Pranit feel being picked because of his glasses?
qa.a: Pranit may feel pressure to be a genius and embarrassed when he freezes, since he had never done this kind of puzzle.

grounding: A maths club helper describes a girl at a maths club who picks a quiet boy with glasses as her partner and turns away a loud boy who then wins.

passage: Karthik, you called that new boy a nerd because of his glasses, na? Come, sit with your Neelam paati for a minute. When I was ten, in our Madurai school, there were two boys in my row. Venkat wore thick glasses and never spoke, so I was sure he was the class first. Balu shouted jokes all day, so I was sure he was the class last. When I had to choose a partner for the maths competition, I picked Venkat and felt very clever. We came fourth. Balu and his partner won the whole district. Later I found out Venkat loved drawing, not sums, and Balu did maths puzzles every night with his father. I had judged both of them by their covers, and I got both covers wrong.

qa.q: Who won the district maths competition?
qa.a: Balu and his partner.

qa.q: Why did young Neelam feel clever choosing Venkat?
qa.a: She felt confident because his glasses and silence matched her picture of a topper, so he seemed a safe choice.

qa.q: At which point in the story could Neelam have chosen better, and how?
qa.a: When picking a maths partner, she could have looked at who actually solved sums in class, instead of going by glasses and noise.

qa.q: How might Venkat have felt being picked for maths?
qa.a: Venkat might have felt pressured and uneasy, since he loved drawing, not sums, and was chosen for his glasses.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how, at ten, she assumed a quiet boy with glasses was the topper and a loud boy was weak, and got both wrong.

passage: "Two minutes to pick your quiz partner, captains!" called Madhuri ma'am. Rain was drumming on the tin roof and half the class was absent with flu, so Omkar had only four boys to choose from. He looked fast. Chirag, quiet, round glasses, always reading: surely a genius. Rakesh, who made silly noises during assembly: surely hopeless. "Chirag!" Omkar said. In the quiz, Chirag froze at every buzzer. Rakesh, on the other team, answered six science questions in a row, laughing loudly each time. At the break Omkar muttered, "But he looks like a topper." Chirag heard and shrugged. "I like reading stories, not science." Omkar went red and didn't know where to look.

qa.q: How many questions in a row did Rakesh answer?
qa.a: Six science questions.

qa.q: Why did Omkar go red at the break?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, because Chirag heard him say he looked like a topper, and it was clear the glasses had not meant what Omkar thought.

qa.q: What could Omkar try next time he picks a team, even in a hurry?
qa.a: Think of who actually answered well in past science lessons, instead of who looks clever.

qa.q: What is it like for Chirag to be picked for his glasses?
qa.a: Chirag probably felt awkward and under pressure, freezing at the buzzer in a quiz about something he doesn't love.

grounding: In a rushed quiz pick, a boy chooses a quiet classmate with glasses as the genius and writes off a noisy one, who turns out strong.

passage: In the colony clubhouse in Kolkata, the summer chess camp paired players by drawing names. Tanvir drew Arnab, the loud boy who sang film songs on the swings. He grinned. "Easy win." His sister Vandana drew Subho, quiet, thick glasses, a book under his arm. "Bad luck, didi," Tanvir whispered. "He'll finish you." Twenty minutes later Vandana had checkmated Subho, who admitted he only came because his mother made him. Tanvir was still at his board, sweating. Arnab had taken his queen with a knight and was humming while he waited. "How are you so good?" Tanvir asked. "My nani and I play every night," said Arnab. Tanvir stared at the board, then at Arnab's grin, and tried to remember why he'd been so sure.

qa.q: What piece did Arnab take with a knight?
qa.a: Tanvir's queen.

qa.q: Why was Tanvir so sure he would beat Arnab?
qa.a: He felt confident because loud, singing Arnab didn't match his idea of a clever player, while quiet Subho with glasses did.

qa.q: What could Tanvir do before the next camp game?
qa.a: Watch how players actually play, or ask about their practice, instead of judging from glasses or singing.

qa.q: What might Vandana make of Tanvir's warning after her game?
qa.a: She would likely find it funny, since the boy Tanvir said would finish her lost to her in twenty minutes.

grounding: At a chess camp, a boy assumes the quiet boy with glasses is the strong player and the loud singer is weak, and is proved wrong.

passage:
"Farida didi, the new boy in my class is going to be the topper."
"Which one, Kamal?"
"The quiet one with thick glasses. He looks like a topper."
"How do you know he's clever?"
"He wears glasses. And he doesn't talk."
"Hmm. And the other new boy?"
"Mohan? He's always shouting and joking. He'll probably fail."
"Did you see their marks?"
"No. But you can tell."
A week later.
"Didi! Didi! Guess what?"
"What?"
"Mohan got the highest in maths! And the glasses boy got less than me!"
"But you said you could tell."
Kamal scratched his head. "I thought I could."

qa.q: Who got the highest in maths?
qa.a: Mohan.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel sure the quiet boy would be the topper?
qa.a: Glasses and silence matched Kamal's idea of a clever student, so it felt like proof, and he was surprised when it wasn't true.

qa.q: What could Kamal do next time he meets someone new?
qa.a: He could wait to see what they actually do in class, like their answers and marks, before deciding how clever they are.

qa.q: How might Mohan feel if he knew Kamal expected him to fail?
qa.a: Mohan might feel hurt or annoyed at being judged for being loud.

grounding: It shows a child who assumes the quiet boy with glasses is clever and the loud boy is weak, until real marks prove otherwise.

passage: In Class 4, when two new boys joined, I was sure I knew all about them from one look. Jeetu wore glasses and sat quietly at the front. I thought, he's the topper type. Bunty sat at the back, laughing loudly and drumming on the desk. I thought, he'll get zero. I even told my friends. Then Urmila ma'am gave a surprise test. Bunty got full marks. Jeetu got six out of ten. I was so surprised that I asked Urmila ma'am if she'd mixed up the papers. She laughed and said, "Omkar, you can't see a brain through glasses." I felt a bit silly. After that, I started waiting to see what people did before deciding.

qa.q: How many marks did Jeetu get in the surprise test?
qa.a: Six out of ten.

qa.q: Why was Omkar so sure about Jeetu and Bunty at first?
qa.a: The glasses and quietness matched Omkar's picture of a topper, and the laughing matched a weak student, so it felt certain, and later Omkar felt surprised and silly.

qa.q: What did Omkar change after the test?
qa.a: Omkar started waiting to see what people actually did before deciding what they were like.

qa.q: How might Urmila ma'am have felt when Omkar asked if she mixed up the papers?
qa.a: Urmila ma'am seemed amused and used the moment to teach gently.

grounding: It shows a child who judges two new classmates by their look and manner, until test results show appearance isn't evidence.

passage:
Class 3 note, Tuesday

During group work today, Karthik refused to be in a group with Rohit. "He's loud and messy. He'll be bad at maths." He wanted Arun instead, "because Arun wears glasses and is quiet, so he's clever."

I let the groups stay mixed. In the maths game, Rohit solved the puzzle first, shouting with excitement. Arun got stuck and asked Karthik for help.

After class, Karthik came up to me looking confused. "Ma'am, Rohit is good at maths?" I asked him how he had decided before. He said, "He looked like he wouldn't be." I told him that the best way to know is to see what someone does.

I'll keep mixing groups this week.

— Ankita

qa.q: Who solved the puzzle first in the maths game?
qa.a: Rohit.

qa.q: Why did Karthik feel so sure Arun was clever?
qa.a: Arun's glasses and quietness matched Karthik's idea of a clever child, so it felt like proof, and later he felt confused and surprised.

qa.q: What was wise about Ankita's decision to keep groups mixed?
qa.a: It let Karthik see real evidence of what each child could do, which is better than telling him he was wrong.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel if he knew why Karthik didn't want him in the group?
qa.a: Rohit might feel hurt at being judged as bad at maths for being loud.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, a child who assumes a quiet boy with glasses is clever and a loud boy weak, until he sees real evidence.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Winter camp, day 2.

Today we got teams for the camp quiz. My team has Santosh and a boy called Nirav.

Nirav is quiet and has thick glasses and reads all the time. I thought YES, he'll know everything. Santosh never stops talking and jumps around. I thought, oh no.

Then the quiz started. Nirav didn't know the capital of Australia. Santosh knew almost everything! Planets, cricket scores, old kings. He got us seven points alone.

At dinner I told Santosh I thought he'd be bad. He laughed and said everyone thinks that because he's loud.

I felt bad. I only looked at their faces and decided.

Tomorrow is the treasure hunt. I'm not guessing anymore.

Gautam

qa.q: How many points did Santosh get the team?
qa.a: He got us seven points alone.

qa.q: How did Gautam feel after telling Santosh about the wrong guess?
qa.a: Gautam felt bad and a little ashamed, realising the judgement came only from how the boys looked and acted.

qa.q: What could Gautam do at the treasure hunt instead of guessing?
qa.a: Gautam could wait to see what each teammate actually knows or can do before deciding who is good at what.

qa.q: How does Santosh seem to feel about being misjudged?
qa.a: Santosh laughs it off, but he seems used to it, which suggests it has happened often and may sometimes sting.

grounding: A child assumes the quiet boy with glasses will be the quiz star and the loud boy weak, until the quiz shows otherwise.

passage:
The rains had closed the fields around the village, so the headmaster announced a maths contest in the school hall. Salma watched the boys line up.

Rehan, quiet, with round glasses and his shirt tucked in, stood near the front. Omkar, who shouted in class and always had mud on his feet, pushed in at the back.

Salma was sure. Rehan would win. Omkar would come last.

Rehan got two, then went silent. Omkar kept shouting answers, most of them right. By the end, Omkar had won.

Her friend beside her shrugged. "He helps his father at the vegetable stall every Sunday. He counts money all day."

Salma felt her face go warm. She had only looked at the glasses and the mud.

qa.q: Why is Omkar good at adding numbers, according to Salma's friend?
qa.a: He helps his father at the vegetable stall every Sunday and counts money all day.

qa.q: Why did Salma's face go warm at the end?
qa.a: Salma felt embarrassed, realising she had judged the boys only by the glasses and the mud, not by what they could do.

qa.q: What could Salma do next time before deciding who is clever?
qa.a: Salma could wait to see what people actually do, or ask about their skills, instead of guessing from how they look.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel if he knew what Salma had assumed?
qa.a: Omkar might feel hurt or annoyed, but also proud that his win proved her wrong.

grounding: During the monsoon, a child assumes the quiet boy with glasses will win and the loud muddy boy will lose, and is surprised.

passage:
It was the last week before Christmas in Madrid, and the class was doing a times-table race for a box of turrón.

Camila looked around. Mateo, small and quiet, with glasses, sat perfectly still. Felix, who never stopped talking and got told off daily, was spinning his pencil.

Mateo will win, Camila decided. He looks like he knows maths. Felix is probably terrible.

The teacher called out: "Seven times eight!" Felix's hand shot up. "Fifty-six!" "Nine times six!" "Fifty-four!" Mateo got one.

Felix won the turrón.

At break, Camila asked Mateo, "Why didn't you answer?"

"I'm not really good at times tables. I like drawing."

Camila bit into her piece of turrón. She had been so sure, just from his glasses.

qa.q: What was the prize for the times-table race?
qa.a: A box of turrón.

qa.q: Why was Camila so sure Mateo would win?
qa.a: Camila felt confident because Mateo's glasses and quietness looked like a maths person, so appearance felt like proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Camila for the next class contest?
qa.a: Don't pick a winner by looks; see what each person actually does, or ask them what they like.

qa.q: How might Mateo feel when people expect him to be the maths star?
qa.a: Mateo might feel pressured and shy, especially when he likes drawing more than times tables.

grounding: A child abroad assumes the quiet boy with glasses will be best at maths and the loud boy worst, and is proved wrong.

passage:
On the first day after the summer holidays, the Class 4 room smelled of new books and rain. The teacher, Vandana ma'am, said there would be a quick maths quiz in pairs.
Farhan looked around. There was Kunal, quiet, thin, with thick glasses, reading a comic in the corner. And there was Bunty, the loud boy who drummed on the desk and laughed at everything.
Farhan grabbed Kunal's arm. "You're with me." He was sure the boy with glasses was the topper. Bunty got paired with Ritu.
The quiz started. Kunal stared at the questions and whispered, "I'm bad at maths." Across the room, Bunty was scribbling answers and cheering. Bunty and Ritu won.
Farhan sat there, stunned. "But he looks so... noisy."
Vandana ma'am, collecting the sheets, smiled. "Looks don't do sums, Farhan."

qa.q: Who won the maths quiz?
qa.a: Bunty and Ritu won the quiz.

qa.q: Why was Farhan so sure Kunal would be the topper?
qa.a: Farhan felt confident because Kunal was quiet and wore thick glasses, so he looked like a topper, and that look felt like proof.

qa.q: What could Farhan do next time before choosing a partner?
qa.a: He could ask classmates about their real strengths or remember past results, instead of judging by how someone looks or acts.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel being picked because of his glasses?
qa.a: Kunal might feel pressured and embarrassed, knowing he isn't good at maths and that Farhan expected him to be.

grounding: It shows a child assuming the quiet boy with glasses must be the topper and the loud boy must be weak, as appearance stands in for real evidence.
